rationale: Both texts say that prophets of the past wanted what the present hearers now have: “many prophets and righteous men longed to see what you see but did not see it” (Matthew 13:17, BSB) and “the prophets who foretold the grace to come to you searched and investigated carefully” and “were not serving themselves, but you” (1 Peter 1:10, 12, BSB). The Expositor’s Greek Testament, on 1 Peter 1:10-12, holds that “St. Peter has utilised a saying of Jesus,” and Ellicott writes that “Precisely the same argument is used for precisely the same purpose by our Lord in Matthew 13:16-17”; that published reading is the evidence for typing it as an allusion rather than only a shared theme. The closest precedent is conn-matt5-james2-poor (allusion/plausible: a later NT writer echoing a saying of Jesus without naming it). The label is plausible, not strong, because the wording barely overlaps: Peter’s prophets “searched and investigated,” and the one shared verb (Greek epithymeo, BSB “longed” / “long”) is used in 1 Peter of angels (“Even angels long to look into these things,” 1:12), not of prophets. The Expositor’s Greek Testament’s own account of how “righteous” could have become “angels” is a conjecture this lesson does not test.
